topic.subject: science
topic.title: The cell
topic.scope: cell as basic unit, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, plant vs animal cells, organelles, unicellular vs multicellular

concepts.name: Cell as the basic unit of life

misconceptions.statement: Cells are only found in living things that are small enough to be seen under a microscope.
misconceptions.why: Students associate the term 'cell' with the microscopic scale and struggle to grasp that large organisms are composed of billions of them.
misconceptions.fix: All living organisms, regardless of their size, are made up of cells. Large organisms are simply multicellular, meaning they contain many cells working together.

probe.question: Is a large banyan tree made of cells like a tiny amoeba?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only tiny things like amoeba are made of cells; large things are made of solid matter.

misconceptions.statement: Cells are like little bricks that just stack together to give an organism its shape.
misconceptions.why: The common textbook analogy of cells as 'building blocks' leads students to view them as static, inert structural components rather than dynamic, living units.
misconceptions.fix: Cells are living units that perform life processes like respiration and digestion; they are not just structural bricks.

probe.question: Do cells inside your body do anything besides holding your shape?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are just like bricks in a wall that keep the body together.

misconceptions.statement: The nucleus is the 'brain' of the cell that thinks and makes decisions.
misconceptions.why: Anthropomorphic language used in textbooks to explain the nucleus's control function leads students to attribute human-like cognitive abilities to organelles.
misconceptions.fix: The nucleus acts as a control center by storing genetic information that regulates cell activities, but it does not 'think' or make conscious decisions.

probe.question: How does the nucleus know when to tell the cell to divide?
probe.wrong_answer: It thinks about it and decides when the cell needs to grow.

misconceptions.statement: All cells have the same organelles regardless of the organism.
misconceptions.why: Students often generalize the 'typical' animal cell diagram to all living things, ignoring the diversity of cell types.
misconceptions.fix: Different cells have different organelles; for example, plant cells have chloroplasts and cell walls, which animal cells lack.

probe.question: Do all cells in your body have chloroplasts?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all cells have the same parts like chloroplasts and mitochondria.

misconceptions.statement: Plant cells do not have a cell membrane because they have a cell wall.
misconceptions.why: Students often think that the presence of a rigid wall replaces the need for a membrane, confusing the two structures.
misconceptions.fix: Plant cells have both a cell wall for protection and a cell membrane to regulate the movement of substances in and out of the cell.

probe.question: Does a plant cell have a cell membrane?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it only has a cell wall to protect it.
